title: Cycle Frequency (Hz), Period (T = 1/f) and Binary Bits (2^N)

blocks.x: Goal

Convert between a repeating signal's **frequency** ($f$, in Hertz `Hz`) and its **period** ($T = 1/f$, in seconds), and use **powers of 2** ($2^N$) to calculate the exact integer range of an $N$-bit microcontroller register.

items.x: **New ideas (max 2):**
**Cycle frequency (`Hz`) and period ($T = 1/f$)**: Relating how many cycles happen per second (`Hz`) to the time duration of a single cycle ($T = \frac{1}{f}$).
**Binary bits and powers of 2 ($2^N$)**: Why $N$ digital bits (`0` or `1`) represent $2^N$ distinct integers from `0` to $2^N - 1$ (explaining `0..255` for 8-bit and `0..1023` for 10-bit).
**New syntax:** `1.0 / freq_hz`, `(2 ** n_bits) - 1`.
**Target time (unmeasured — [log yours](../.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/beginner-timing-log.md)):** Typical: 1.0–1.5 hours | Slow-learner: 2.0–3.0 hours

blocks.x: Idea 1: Cycle frequency (`Hz`) and period ($T = 1/f$)

items.x: **Primary resource:** [The Physics Classroom — Frequency and Period of a Wave](https://www.physicsclassroom.com/class/waves/Lesson-2/Frequency-and-Period-of-a-Wave) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]`
**What to read:** Read exact heading **`Frequency and Period of a Wave`** (specifically the reciprocal formulas $f = 1/T$ and $T = 1/f$).
**What to skip:** Skip the bottom pendulum/mass-on-a-spring practice questions once $T = 1/f$ is clear.

**Key takeaway:** **Frequency** ($f$, measured in **Hertz `Hz`**, where $1\text{ Hz} = 1\text{ cycle per second}$) counts how many times a control loop or switching signal repeats each second. **Period** ($T$, measured in seconds `s`) is the time duration of *one* cycle. They are exact reciprocals: $T = \frac{1}{f}$ and $f = \frac{1}{T}$.

blocks.x: Idea 2: Binary bits and powers of 2 ($2^N$)

items.x: **Primary resource:** [SparkFun — Binary](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/binary) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]`
**What to read:** Read exact headings **`Why Binary?`**, **`Counting in binary`**, and **`Converting binary to decimal`**.
**What to skip:** Skip **`Bitwise Operators`**, **`Hexadecimal`**, and **`Two's Complement`** (not needed until Track 04).

**Key takeaway:** Digital circuits store numbers using **bits** (binary digits that are either `0` for OFF or `1` for ON). Each extra bit doubles the number of possible combinations, so an **$N$-bit** register has **$2^N$ states** numbered from **`0` up to $2^N - 1$**.

**Unsigned:** those counts are **unsigned integers** — whole numbers with **no sign bit**, because all $N$ bits count towards the magnitude. Nothing in the register says "minus", so the range is $0$ to $2^N - 1$ and there is no negative value to return: `max_unsigned_int(8)` is `255`, not `127`. A *signed* register spends its top bit on the sign instead, which is why a signed byte stops at `127`. Motor commands and sensor counts are unsigned — a duty cycle has no negative direction, a direction pin carries the sign — so this lesson's second function is named `max_unsigned_int` on purpose.

**Alternative resource:** [MathsIsFun — Binary Number System](https://www.mathsisfun.com/binary-number-system.html) `[HTTP 200 — Verified by scripts/check_links.py]` — Read exact headings **`How do we Count using Binary?`** and **`Position`** (powers of 2: $1, 2, 4, 8, 16, \dots$).

blocks.x: Micro focus: period is the reciprocal of frequency

Frequency (`f`, in hertz `Hz`) counts cycles per second, and period (`T`) is the seconds one cycle takes. They describe the same tick from opposite sides: `T = 1 / f` and `f = 1 / T`, so 50 Hz is a 0.02 s period and a 0.01 s period is 100 Hz.
Micro focus: each bit doubles the states
A bit holds 0 or 1, and an N-bit register has 2^N states, numbered from 0 to 2^N - 1. Eight bits give 256 states from 0 to 255, which is exactly why a motor command register stops at 255.
Micro focus: what an unsigned integer is

An **unsigned integer** is a whole number that cannot go below zero: no minus sign, no decimal point. Eight bits make $2^8 = 256$ different on/off patterns — `0000 0000`, `0000 0001`, `0000 0010`, … `1111 1111` — and numbering those patterns from zero makes the last one `255`. That is the whole idea: every bit is spent on how big the number is, and no bit is held back to mean "negative". So $N$ bits hold the whole numbers `0` to $2^N - 1$, and `-1` is simply not one of them. A register that *does* keep its top bit for the sign is called **signed**, which is why a signed byte stops at `127`; the motor commands and sensor counts this course reads are all unsigned.
Micro focus: place values double
Read binary with its place values: the place values are `1, 2, 4, 8, ...`, doubling to the left, and a 1 adds that value while a 0 adds nothing. So 1011 is 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11, and 1000 is 8.
Bridge Notes
Two sets of numbers appear in almost every microcontroller program you will ever write:
First, **frequency ($f$)** and **period ($T$)** are two ways of describing the same clock tick:

items.x: A standard hobby pulse repeats at $f = 50\text{ Hz}$, so each cycle lasts $T = \frac{1}{50\text{ Hz}} = 0.020\text{ s} = 20\text{ ms}$.
A fast robot control loop runs at $f = 1\text{ kHz}$ ($1{,}000\text{ Hz}$), so each time step is $T = \frac{1}{1000\text{ Hz}} = 0.001\text{ s} = 1.0\text{ ms}$.

blocks.x: Second, **binary bits ($2^N$)** explain why microcontrollers use seemingly strange maximum numbers like `255` and `1023` instead of `100` or `1000`:

items.x: **8-bit register** (1 **byte**, used by 8-bit output commands): $2^8 = 256$ states $\rightarrow$ integers **`0` to `255`** ($2^8 - 1$).
**10-bit register** (used by 10-bit sensor inputs): $2^{10} = 1{,}024$ states $\rightarrow$ integers **`0` to `1023`** ($2^{10} - 1$).
**12-bit register** (used by 12-bit sensor inputs in later tracks): $2^{12} = 4{,}096$ states $\rightarrow$ integers **`0` to `4095`** ($2^{12} - 1$).

blocks.x: Because counting starts at `0`, the maximum integer is always **$2^N - 1$**.

**Unsigned** is the word for that range: all $N$ bits count the number, so there is no room for a minus sign, and 8 bits give `0` to `255`. A byte that stopped at `127` was *signed* — its top bit meant "negative". Both values this lesson computes are unsigned by nature, a count and a motor command, which is why `max_unsigned_int` returns $2^N - 1$.

In `TODO 1`, `1.0 / freq_hz` gives seconds, and multiplying by `1000.0` converts seconds to milliseconds (`ms`). In `TODO 2`, use `**` for powers of 2: `(2 ** n_bits) - 1`.

blocks.text:
def freq_to_period_ms(freq_hz):
    return (1.0 / freq_hz) * 1000.0


def max_unsigned_int(n_bits):
    return (2 ** n_bits) - 1


assert round(freq_to_period_ms(50.0), 2) == 20.00
assert round(freq_to_period_ms(490.0), 3) == 2.041
assert max_unsigned_int(8) == 255
assert max_unsigned_int(10) == 1023
assert max_unsigned_int(12) == 4095

print(f"50 Hz period: {freq_to_period_ms(50.0):.2f} ms | 490 Hz period: {freq_to_period_ms(490.0):.3f} ms")
print(f"8-bit max: {max_unsigned_int(8)} | 10-bit max: {max_unsigned_int(10)} | 12-bit max: {max_unsigned_int(12)}")

blocks.x: Common mistakes & troubleshooting

items.x: **Saying an 8-bit register goes up to `256` instead of `255`:** There are $2^8 = 256$ total values, but because `0` uses the first slot, the highest number is $256 - 1 = \mathbf{255}$.

**Forgetting to convert `kHz` to `Hz` before taking $1/f$:** For a $20\text{ kHz}$ switching wave, convert $20\text{ kHz} = 20{,}000\text{ Hz}$ first so $T = \frac{1}{20{,}000} = 0.00005\text{ s} = 50\ \mu\text{s}$.

blocks.x: Check yourself

items.x: **Period to frequency:** A control loop executes once every $T = 0.5\text{ ms}$ ($0.0005\text{ s}$). What is its frequency $f$ in `Hz` and in `kHz`?

blocks.x: $f = \frac{1}{0.0005\text{ s}} = \mathbf{2{,}000\text{ Hz}} = \mathbf{2.0\text{ kHz}}$.

items.x: **Why `1023`?** In one sentence, explain why a 10-bit sensor register returns a maximum of `1023` instead of `1000`.

blocks.x: Because a 10-bit binary register has $2^{10} = 1{,}024$ possible states, and starting the count at `0` makes the highest state $1024 - 1 = \mathbf{1023}$.

items.x: **4-bit range:** How many total states does a 4-bit binary number have, and what is its maximum integer value?

blocks.x: $2^4 = \mathbf{16\text{ states}}$, ranging from `0` to $2^4 - 1 = \mathbf{15}$.
Recap

items.x: **Frequency ($f$, in `Hz`)** and **period ($T$, in `s`)** are reciprocals: $T = \frac{1}{f}$ and $f = \frac{1}{T}$.
An **$N$-bit** binary register stores $2^N$ integers from **`0` to $2^N - 1$** (`0..255` for 8-bit, `0..1023` for 10-bit).
